newsitem.title: USA: Bowles no stranger to Whitewater, Morris scandals.
newsitem.headline: Bowles no stranger to Whitewater, Morris scandals.

text.p: North Carolina businessman Erskine Bowles, President Bill Clinton's new chief of staff, is a former White House aide and a Clinton confidant well versed in controversies that have dogged the president.
Clinton announced on Friday that Bowles, 51, will replace Leon Panetta, who is leaving the administration to return to his native California.

The chief of staff is the most powerful position in the White House, coordinating policy in the executive branch and controlling access to the president. The choice of chief of staff does not require Senate approval.

As deputy chief in 1995, Bowles was reported to be the aide who told Clinton that Dick Morris, his most senior and trusted re-election campaign strategist, had had a long-running extramarital affair with a woman in Texas that produced an out-of-wedlock daughter.

Clinton also turned to Bowles, a close friend and occasional golf partner, for more information on Morris during this year's Democratic National Convention in Chicago in August, after tabloid newspaper reports of an ongoing liaison between Morris and a prostitute.

Bowles subsequently met with Morris at Clinton's behest and Morris resigned on the last day of the convention, casting a pall on Clinton's acceptance of his party's nomination for president but also resolving a major staff problem for him.

In 1995, when he was still a White House aide, Bowles went before the Senate Whitewater Committee to answer questions about a small business loan made to former Clinton business partner Susan McDougal. She was jailed this year for refusing to testify about Clinton's role in the complex web of bank and real estate dealings known as Whitewater.

Bowles, who ran the federal Small Business Administration in 1993-94, gave investigators little specific information when asked about accusations that the White House got confidential information from the SBA about Clinton's chief Whitewater accuser, former Arkansas municipal judge David Hale.
Hale alleged that Clinton pressured him to help with a small business loan for Susan McDougal. Hale, later indicted, said the $300,000 government-backed loan was fraudulent.

Bowles, who was named deputy White House chief of staff in 1994 and left to start a venture capital firm in December 1995, raised money in the South to help elect Clinton in 1992, and gained a reputation as a Clinton loyalist at the SBA.

Small business lobbyists credited him with accelerating lending practices of the often-criticised agency and for having gained Clinton's ear as a member of the policy-shaping National Economic Council.
He shipped out scores of SBA workers from the Washington headquarters to offices around the country to speed up loan disbursements and built up lending to women and minorities.

But Bowles annoyed small business groups with his advocacy of Hillary Rodham Clinton's health care reform plan which was widely opposed by owners of small businesses because they said it would tax them too heavily.

Born August 8, 1945, Bowles worked in investment banking in New York until 1975, when he left to co-found a bank -- Hollowell Conner & Co -- in his native North Carolina to lend to small and middle-sized businesses.
Since 1996, he has been a partner in Carousel Capital Co. in Charlotte, N.C.
His wife Crandall is a top executive of Springs Industries in North Carolina, a textiles firm her family founded.
They have three children, two boys and a girl. His son Sam has diabetes, and Bowles has served as the international president of the Juvenile Diabetes Foundation.
